name: Turmeric (topical)
lead: Topical turmeric refers to the use of turmeric root (Curcuma longa) or its main pigment curcumin on the skin, as a paste, mask or cream. It is a long-standing household and traditional preparation in South Asia, promoted in appearance communities as a brightening, evening and anti-blemish ingredient.

Published human research on topical turmeric for skin appearance is sparse. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study tested a turmeric cream in vitiligo, a condition of pigment loss, and reported in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology in 2022.[1] That study concerns a medical skin condition rather than general brightening, and no trial of turmeric for skin lightening in healthy skin appears in the sources reviewed.

Turmeric is a strong yellow dye. Case literature documents yellow skin discolouration after oral turmeric supplements,[2] and the pigment's staining effect is a recognised practical feature of its topical use.

paras: Turmeric is used in home preparations applied to the face and body in several cultures, usually as a paste mixed with a liquid such as milk, yoghurt or water, with the stated aim of a brighter, more even complexion. Commercial creams and gels containing turmeric or curcumin extract are also marketed. The compound is described in the vitiligo study as having been widely examined for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-proliferative properties, which is the usual rationale given for topical use.[1]

A 2022 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial evaluated a topical turmeric cream in people with vitiligo.[1] It is the only human trial of topical turmeric in a pigmentation context found in the sources reviewed, and it addresses repigmentation of a disease rather than cosmetic skin brightening.

Registered trials of topical curcumin products exist for other conditions, including oral lichen planus,[3] psoriasis,[4] periodontitis,[5] seborrhoeic dermatitis and dry scalp,[6] and cervical lesions.[7] None of these tests skin lightening or complexion evenness.

Turmeric pigment stains skin, nails and fabric yellow. A case report described a 68-year-old woman whose soles turned yellow after about four months of a daily oral turmeric root capsule; the colour faded after she stopped.[2] That report concerns oral supplementation rather than topical use. Controlled data on irritation or allergic reactions to topical turmeric are not available in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Traditional yellow spice paste used for brightening; one small vitiligo trial exists, none for cosmetic lightening, and it stains.
card.note: Stains skin yellow; the only pigment-related trial is a pilot in vitiligo.

quick.overview:
Topical turmeric means applying turmeric root or its pigment curcumin to the skin, usually as a paste or cream. It is a traditional brightening and blemish remedy, especially in South Asia.

The human research is thin. One randomised pilot trial tested a turmeric cream in vitiligo, and other trials of curcumin products cover unrelated conditions. No trial of cosmetic skin lightening was found.
quick.mechanism: Curcumin has been studied for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-proliferative activity, which is the usual rationale for use. Whether this alters pigmentation in healthy skin has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Turmeric stains skin and fabric yellow. Yellow discolouration has been reported with oral supplements. Controlled safety data for topical cosmetic use are lacking.
